newsitem.title: USA: Study shows wide range of car airbag safety.
newsitem.headline: Study shows wide range of car airbag safety.

text.p: Automobile airbags that deploy vertically up the windshield are safer than airbags that pop out horizontally toward the passenger, consumer advocates said on Thursday.

Forty-three deaths -- 40 of them children -- have been linked to low-speed crashes in which airbags inflated directly into the passenger's chest or face. No deaths have been linked to vertically inflating airbags used on several models by Honda and Nissan and the 1996-97 Ford Taurus, according to a study by Public Citizen and the Center for Auto Safety.

"This study shows some airbags are much better than others. Consumers will want to know which type they have in their cars before deciding whether to turn them off," Joan Claybrook, president of Public Citizen, told a news conference.

But an official with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said that while vertical versus horizontal deployment may be a factor in the airbag's safety, it did not appear to be the overriding issue. A number of other factors also were important, he said.
He also said that in virtually every case in which a person died because of an airbag the person was not wearing a seatbelt or was improperly restrained.

"A disservice would be done if people thought that simply because they have a vertical-release bag they should start ignoring precautions of making sure all children 12 and under sit in the back seat and that all occupants are properly restrained (with seat belts)," Phil Recht, NHTSA deputy administrator, said.

Brian O'Neill, president of the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, which represents car insurance companies, said a child who is very close to an airbag when it starts to deploy is at risk, regardless of deployment direction.

The consumer advocates' study said deaths occurred in vehicles with front-deploying airbags that had "an inadequate safety zone" for the passenger. It said those included Chrysler's Dodge Caravan, Ford's Aspire, Contour, Escort and Mustang and General Motors' Geo Metro.

Because of deaths linked to airbags that may slam into passengers, the NHTSA is evaluating whether to allow consumers to deactivate passenger airbags. The consumer advocates said they opposed a broad government authorization to deactivate airbags, saying that would increase risks for most consumers.

But they said the government must do more to inform consumers of differences in airbags including issues such as rates of inflation, sensor performance, the minimum vehicle speed upon impact that will trigger inflation of the airbag, and the type of deployment of the airbag.

"Our study suggests that some designs reduce fatalities but the government needs to tell the public exactly which cars have the safest airbags," Clarence Ditlow, executive director of the Center for Auto Safety, said.
However an NHTSA official said experts still were trying to understand airbag safety differences and said it would be premature to issue government rankings.

Claybrook said consumers should ask the dealer or manufacturer how the passenger airbag deploys and factor that into a car-buying decision. Not all bags mounted on top of the dashboard deploy vertically but almost all that are mounted on the front of the dashboard deploy horizontally, she said.

The consumer groups also said manufacturers should use available technology to raise the deployment threshold on the passenger airbag to 15 miles (24 km) per hour rather than matching the eight or nine mph threshold needed to protect the driver from hitting the steering column.

They also said manufacturers should use better sensors that do not trigger below the threshold speed or late in the crash, deep-dish steering wheels to move the airbag away from the driver and airbag compartmentalization and fold patterns to avoid injury to passengers who are out of position.
